newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Australian race debate sends a ripple through Asia.
newsitem.headline: Australian race debate sends a ripple through Asia.

text.p: Australia's acrimonious race debate has sent a ripple through Asia, reinforcing views of a country grappling with old demons while delicately expanding diplomatic and trade ties with its neighbours.
But few officials and ordinary citizens in Asia expect Australia's backlash against Asian immigration -- led by race row politician Pauline Hanson -- to affect trade ties.
"I won't stop buying Australian beef or boycott Australian products just because of a discriminatory drive by a short-sighted woman," said Julia Huang, 58, a translator in Taiwan.

Hanson has called for a freeze on immigration, arguing in her maiden speech to parliament that Australia risked being "swamped by Asians" who have "their own culture and religion and form ghettos and do not assimilate".
The independent legislator tapped a nerve in a country which only abandoned a "white Australia" immigration policy in the late 1960s.

Her recently formed One Nation Party has attracted strong support and now ranks as the country's third most popular party, well ahead of Australia's traditional third political force, the Australian Democrats.
Canberra has stepped up criticism of Hanson in recent months, describing her views as stupid, but her rallies draw thousands of supporters, along with thousands of protesters.

The issue has been cited as a threat to Australia's trade and investment links, but a random selection of views across Asia showed most people reserving judgement on the country, although the debate has revived fears of racism for some.

"I know Australia can have a very white point of view and that some people support this, but I never thought that the majority felt this way," said Anne Lee, an office worker in Hong Kong. "If she gets majority support, then I might change my opinion about Australia, and think it practices racial discrimination."
Wai Haw-Yinn, a Malaysian who spent 11 years in Australian schools, said she has watched the Hanson debate with some concern.

"I was considering going back to live and now it has made me think about it in the current circumstances. I would probably go back, but before I wouldn't have thought twice about it," said the 30-year-old teacher.
About 13,000 Malaysian students study in Australia at any one time.
Some Taiwanese voiced concern about relatives in Australia.
"I worry that the campaign will affect my husband's business in Australia," said secretary Elsie Fang, adding that she would ask her son to return from Australia where he has been studying.
Wayne Hsu, emigration consultant of Fastlane International Corp in Taiwan, said Hanson's campaign had discouraged a number of students from studying in Australia.
"At least 20 percent of Taiwan students cancelled their plans to study in Australia in the past year under the insistence of their worried parents," he said.
At the same time, the rate of study in Canada has risen, he said, without giving figures.
Taiwan's Board of Foreign Trade said two-way trade had not been affected by Hanson's campaign.
An Australian embassy official in Tokyo said the reaction in Japan towards the Hanson issue has so far been muted.
"It hasn't rung alarm bells yet, not to say that it might not if the One Nation's party's policies were seen to have some enduring popular support," he said.

"Obviously publicity of this kind does us no good. The longer the wrenching debate goes on in Australia, and if it is seen as being an enduring part of Australia's political landscape, it becomes a negative for our interests in Asia."
Few South Korean newspapers have carried reports on the issue and Koreans generally seemed uninterested. Australia continues to be a favourite destination for Korean tourists.
Indonesian foreign minister Ali Alatas said last week that Jakarta hoped Hanson's views were not generally shared by most Australians or the country's government.

"We continue to hope that this issue, or this apparent approach of Pauline Hanson, is not going to be spreading because I think that would be detrimental to Australia's relationships not only with Indonesia, but the rest of Southeast Asia... ," he said.

In Thailand, Professor Prathoomporn Vajarathira, from the international relations division of Chulalongkorn University, said he expected Hanson's policies to have a negative impact on Australian interests in Asia.
Prathoomporn however said damage caused by Hanson would be minor because the government seemed aware Australians could not afford to lose interest in Asian people.
Some Singaporeans were dismayed by the support Hanson has received and said they would rather emigrate to a country other than Australia, although the overall issue was considered minor.
"Hanson has made the situation ugly. I don't like it very much there," a trader at a foreign commodity house said.
But the trader, who asked not to be identified, said she would go ahead with her planned holiday in Australia at Christmas but would rather emigrate to Canada than live in Australia.
"For a holiday, it's a beautiful place if you just want to spend your money there. But that's it. I do not want to live there," she said.
The Hanson episode gave the strong impression Asians would get a hostile reception in Australia, she added.
Ishtiaq Hossain, a political scientist lecturer at the National University of Singapore, said he was dissapointed Australian Prime Minister John Howard did not immediately denounce Hanson's views.
But he said most Singaporeans still prefer to attend Australian universities because they cost less than U.S. or European schools.
A spokesman for the Australian High Commission in Singapore said Hanson's remarks had apparently had no impact on companies looking at investing in Australia.
The issue appeared to have barely any impact in India.
An official at a leading New Delhi export-import firm said: "I don't think it is going to have a long lasting effect on trade even though it might somewhat affect the sentiment."
An Australian High Commission official in the Sri Lankan capital, Colombo, said: "We do get asked a few questions sometimes, but overall the situation is not bad here."
